title: Building agent fleet architectures your CISO doesn't hate — Lou Bichard, Gitpod

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary: Lou Bichard, field CTO at Gitpod, discusses building CISO-approved agent fleet architectures for regulated industries. Gitpod is a platform for secure development environments where developers work approximately 37 hours per week, making it mission-critical software serving banks, pharmaceutical companies, and healthcare providers. The talk targets vendors building AI tools, consumers in secure environments, and buyers evaluating architectural options. Gitpod's agent offering was publicly launched two days before the talk after months of design-partner development. The presentation traces Gitpod's architectural evolution across several iterations. The journey began in 2019 with a managed SaaS product on GCP Kubernetes, which suffered crypto mining abuse and was insufficient for enterprise security. Next came a self-hosted model with significant day-2 operational overhead eroding ROI. A substrate model followed—managed service on AWS-only infrastructure—but retained Kubernetes complexity and high fixed costs. Gitpod then moved away from Kubernetes entirely to a runner-based architecture: a single ECS task running secure workloads on customer AWS infrastructure using native EC2 and EBS, costing single-figure dollars monthly. Gitpod retains only non-sensitive metadata like user IDs. Deployment via the runner interface takes as little as 3 minutes, with the main challenge being gathering network configuration details (VPC, subnets) from the customer's organization. This architecture now underpins Gitpod's agent fleet offering, which is privacy-first: agents run inside customer infrastructure with the same access and privileges as human developers, needing source code and internal system access. The API-first design ensures every action—including agent tasks—is audit logged, providing full audit history for regulated customers. Lou advises buyers to evaluate architecture and infrastructure qualities when purchasing AI tools, and vendors to favor simplicity over complex platforms like Kubernetes.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Gitpod Context
sections.summary: Lou introduces himself as field CTO at Gitpod, a platform for secure dev environments where developers work ~37 hours weekly. Gitpod serves regulated industries including banks, pharma, and healthcare. The talk targets vendors, consumers, and buyers of AI tools in secure environments. The agent offering was launched two days prior after months of design-partner development.

sections.title: Architecture Evolution Overview
sections.summary: Gitpod went through multiple architectural iterations—managed SaaS, self-hosted, substrate, and current model—each with different implications for customer ownership, cost, and security.

sections.title: Managed SaaS on GCP Kubernetes
sections.summary: Starting in 2019, Gitpod ran a managed SaaS on GCP Kubernetes with pods orchestrating dev environments. It offered great one-click UX but suffered crypto mining abuse and was insufficient for enterprise security needs.

sections.title: Self-Hosted Model
sections.summary: Gitpod packaged its architecture for self-hosted installation across various cloud providers and Kubernetes flavors. This created significant day-2 effects: high operational overhead eroding ROI, weak vendor-customer relationships, and unsuccessful adoptions without support.

sections.title: Substrate Model
sections.summary: Gitpod introduced a substrate model: managed service on AWS-only infrastructure with workloads staying on customer side. This reduced variance and operational overhead but retained Kubernetes complexity, multiple clusters, and high fixed costs.

sections.title: Current Runner-Based Architecture
sections.summary: Gitpod moved away from Kubernetes entirely. The current architecture uses a runner—a single ECS task—running secure workloads (source code, data) on customer AWS infrastructure using native EC2 and EBS. The runner costs single-figure dollars monthly. Gitpod retains only non-sensitive metadata (user IDs), not PII or IP. This architecture now underpins the agent fleet offering.

sections.title: Product Demo Introduction
sections.summary: Lou begins a video demonstration (audio off) showing the user experience of selecting workloads, which was cut off at the section boundary.

sections.title: Runner Deployment and Agent Offering
sections.summary: The runner interface simplifies customer onboarding—deployment takes as little as 3 minutes once network details (VPC, subnets) are gathered. Because dev environments serve agents identically to humans (both need source code and internal system access), Gitpod's existing infrastructure directly supports the agent offering. The agent offering is privacy-first, running inside customer infrastructure. The API-first architecture ensures every action is audit logged, extending to agent tasks. Lou closes by advising buyers to evaluate architectural qualities and vendors to favor simplicity over complex platforms like Kubernetes.
